<reflection>
The first experiment provided initial kinetic data, but the negative log-likelihood values for all 20 mechanisms are very close, with M2 having the best fit (-24.38) and M20 the worst (-21.88). The small differences indicate that a single experiment under moderate conditions cannot reliably discriminate among the mechanisms. Many mechanisms—including those with dimerization, activation, or deactivation—fit the data similarly well. The aim of the first turn was to obtain broad initial data, which was achieved. Now, we need a second experiment that will provide complementary information to reduce uncertainty across the entire set of plausible mechanisms.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate among mechanisms, we need to probe how the reaction kinetics scale with catalyst concentration. The first experiment used a moderate catalyst concentration (0.05 M). By reducing the catalyst concentration by an order of magnitude (to 0.005 M) while keeping substrate concentration constant (2.0 M) and no initial product, we can test for non-linear scaling of the reaction rate with catalyst. Mechanisms involving dimerization (e.g., M2, M3, M5, M7, M13, M18, M19) often predict rate laws that depend on [cat]^2 at higher concentrations but may approach linear scaling at low [cat]. Mechanisms with catalyst activation (M6, M8) may show non-linear behavior if the activation equilibrium depends on [cat]. Deactivation mechanisms (e.g., M9–M20) may exhibit different time-course shapes if deactivation steps are bimolecular (e.g., cat+catS in M19), as these steps will be slower at low [cat]. This design avoids extreme conditions (e.g., saturation or depletion) that could mask mechanistic differences and provides a contrast to the first experiment, making it informative for a wide range of candidate mechanisms simultaneously.
</hypothesis>
